name: Victor Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the moulding line at the foundry on Kiln Street, where we cast brake discs for cars and vans. I'm in at six, check the sand mix, warm up the moulding machine and then it's about nine hundred moulds a shift, watching for cracks, cold spots, anything that looks off. I like the rhythm of it and I like the crew, especially Ruben, who's been there thirty-one years and still eats the same cheese roll every day. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the noise, even with the ear defenders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the foundry, and how did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years, since I finished my vocational certificate at eighteen. My uncle got me the interview, and I've never really wanted to be anywhere else. The pay is good for the area because it's hot, dirty work and the union fought hard for the shift rates. I've got my grandmother's old flat, which I own outright, plus about nine months of savings, so I'm not scared of the bills, I just like knowing what tomorrow looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the break room for two years: told you so. Every few months the managers bring in some new screen or system that's meant to change everything, and then we're still the ones fixing the moulds by hand. I'd probably post a sarcastic comment on the union group chat and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the way I like it. Same line, same crew, same pay rise every spring if the union holds firm. I'd be relieved, and I don't mind admitting I'd be a bit smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep putting about a fifth of my pay into savings like I always do, and keep going to the union meetings on the first Tuesday of the month. Maybe Nadia and I would finally take that trip to the coast we keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting home after a long shift and finding nothing has changed while you were gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said management keeps bringing in new screens. Has any of that touched your job so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put a camera on the line last year that's supposed to spot cracked moulds. Half the time it flags a shadow, so Ruben and I just double-check by eye anyway. I don't use any of the AI stuff myself, never have, and nobody's made me yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything about the job you'd want to change anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heat, mainly. The union's been pushing for better cooling fans in the moulding bay for three summers. If AI isn't going to change anything, I'd rather the company spent that money on fans for us than on cameras that can't tell a crack from a shadow.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone at work and on the union chat that I said so all along. AI was always more hype than substance, and we're still the ones keeping the line running.
S0.think: Privately, I'd be relieved and a bit smug. My life stays exactly as I like it, with the same crew, the same pay and no pressure to learn anything new.
S0.do: Keeps working his shifts, saving about a fifth of his pay and going to monthly union meetings. Might finally take the delayed coastal trip with his partner Nadia.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with a little satisfaction at being proved right.
S0.quote: I'd be relieved, and I don't mind admitting I'd be a bit smug about it.
S0.fieldNote: Victor's security comes from routine, a paid-off flat and a strong union, and he clearly enjoys the idea of being proved right. His only gripe is the heat, and he'd rather money went to fans than cameras. He has never used an AI tool and says so with some pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly why we need the union, to make sure the changes are bargained over and not just dumped on us. Online I'd share stuff about protecting workers and keeping humans on the line. I'd be loud about it, because if you're quiet they assume you agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be nervous, because the moulding line is exactly the kind of thing they'd want to automate. But a few years is a long time, and the foundry's been promising a new automatic line since I started. I'd hope I could ride it out until something else came along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal in writing: no one laid off without retraining, and older guys like Ruben protected. I'd keep saving like normal. I wouldn't go off and learn computers or anything, not unless the company made me and paid for it during working hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a strange noise from the machine that you can't quite place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn something new if the company paid. What if they offered a course on running the new automated line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go, as long as it was in paid hours. I'm not against learning, I'm against doing it in my own time so the company can save money. If Ruben's going to be pushed out, I want to be the one who knows the new line so I can keep an eye on things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruben, for sure. He's fifty-nine and he still writes the shift notes in pencil. If they put a touchscreen in front of Ruben, he'd retire the same afternoon, and he can't afford to yet.

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union, to make sure every change is bargained over and not dumped on workers. I'd post about keeping people on the line and protecting jobs.
S1.think: Privately, I'd be nervous because the moulding line is an obvious target for automation. I'd hope a few years of change gives me time to ride it out until something else comes along.
S1.do: Pushes the union for a written deal on retraining and protection for older workers like Ruben. Keeps saving as normal and would only take training if it's in paid hours.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a nagging worry he can't quite pin down yet.
S1.quote: If they put a touchscreen in front of Ruben, he'd retire the same afternoon, and he can't afford to yet.
S1.fieldNote: Victor turns straight to collective action, which fits his politics, and his first worry is for an older colleague rather than himself. He's not against learning, only against doing it unpaid. His plan is mostly to dig in and let the union carry the fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be furious, and I wouldn't hide it. I'd say the companies building this have no right to throw millions of people out of work just because they can, and that governments need to step in and stop it or tax it hard. I'd be at every protest going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means the foundry closes or goes fully robotic, and fast. I've got the flat and the savings, so I wouldn't be on the street, but everything I know how to do would be worth nothing. Nine years learning how sand behaves, and a robot would learn it over a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything extra and move more of my pay into savings. I'd go all in with the union and with whatever campaign was pushing for a tax on robots or a basic income, I'd knock on doors for it. I wouldn't go chasing a new trade, because if this thing can do any job, what would I even train for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake running numbers, even though I know the numbers are fine for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't retrain. With only two years' warning, is there really nothing you'd try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's the point of two years of night school if the robot's ready by the time I finish? I'd rather spend those two years making sure the people who own the robots pay their share. That's a better use of my evenings than learning to code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the night you find out the foundry is going robotic. What do you say to Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not about the money, we'll be fine for a while, it's about what I'd do all day. She works nights at the hospital, so she'd probably say at least I'd finally learn to cook. And she'd be right, but I'd still be gutted.

S2.say: I'd say the companies building this have no right to throw millions out of work just because they can. Governments need to step in and stop it or tax it hard, and I'd be at every protest.
S2.think: Honestly, I think the foundry would close or go fully robotic within months. My flat and savings would keep me afloat, but nine years of skill would be worth nothing.
S2.do: Cuts extra spending and moves more pay into savings straight away. Throws himself into the union and campaigns for a robot tax or basic income, but refuses to retrain because he can't see what he'd train for.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, even though he knows the money would last for a while.
S2.quote: Nine years learning how sand behaves, and a robot would learn it over a weekend.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning, Victor's resistance turns to anger and political action rather than any personal pivot. His money is fine, so what he fears losing is purpose and skill. He also deliberately chooses campaigning over retraining, and he has a reason for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, but I'd also say there's no excuse this time: we can see it coming, so the government had better have a plan. I'd be pushing the union to get every worker a guaranteed income before the robots arrive, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years feels like just enough time to get angry and organised, but not enough to change who I am. I'd be thirty-two, still young, and that scares me more than it would scare Ruben. He gets to retire. I'd have thirty working years with nothing to fill them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe push it up to a third of my pay. I'd take on a bigger role in the union, maybe run for branch secretary. If the foundry offered paid training to look after the robots, I'd take it, but I wouldn't go looking for it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's time to do something, which is almost worse, because then it's on you if you waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives the union time to win something, a deal or a law. With two years it's all panic. With five, I think we could actually force a plan out of the government, and that makes me feel a bit less helpless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only train if the foundry offered. If it never offers, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still be on the line the day the robots arrive, I suppose. I know that sounds stubborn, but I'd rather be the last man on the line than the first one to give up on it. Nadia would probably have something to say about that.

S3.say: I'd say we can see it coming this time, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd push the union to win guaranteed incomes before the robots arrive.
S3.think: Between us, five years feels like enough time to organise but not enough to change who I am. At thirty-two I'd face decades without work, and that scares me more than it would scare Ruben.
S3.do: Raises his savings to about a third of his pay and runs for union branch secretary. Would take company-paid training on the robots but won't seek out new skills himself.
S3.feel: Anxious, because having time makes him feel responsible for using it well.
S3.quote: I know that sounds stubborn, but I'd rather be the last man on the line than the first one to give up on it.
S3.fieldNote: Victor sees the extra time as a political opportunity rather than a personal one. He's quite candid about his stubbornness and seems to know it could hurt him. His age is starting to feel like a burden rather than an advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say this is a test of whether we're a decent society. We've got a decade to make sure the money from all those robots goes to everyone, not just the people who own them. I'd be saying that at work, at the pub and online, every chance I got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is long enough that I'd probably tell myself it's not real yet. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. I'd like to think I'd use the time, but I know myself, and I'd probably keep doing my shifts and hope the union sorts it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the foundry and keep saving. I'd stay active in the union and vote for whoever had a real plan for sharing out the wealth. Maybe around year seven or eight I'd look at what's left, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slow kind. It would sit in the back of my head for ten years like a bill I haven't opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until year seven or eight. What would you be waiting to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the robots actually work in a foundry. Our place is filthy, sand everywhere, molten iron, things break all the time. I'd want to see one survive a summer in the moulding bay before I believed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the ten years would let you do that the two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off nothing, because I owe nothing. But I could help Nadia finish her advanced nursing course, so at least one of us has a job a robot won't want first. That's probably the smartest thing I'd do, and it's for her, not me.

S4.say: I'd say this is a test of whether we're a decent society. We have a decade to make sure the money from robots goes to everyone, not just the owners.
S4.think: Honestly, ten years is long enough that I'd tell myself it isn't real yet. I'd probably keep doing my shifts and hope the union sorts it out.
S4.do: Stays at the foundry, keeps saving and stays active in the union, voting for a party with a plan to share out the gains. Waits until year seven or eight to reassess and helps Nadia finish her nursing course.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow, background way, like an unopened bill.
S4.quote: I'd want to see one survive a summer in the moulding bay before I believed it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Victor openly predicts his own inaction, which is unusually self-aware. His one forward-looking move is supporting his partner's career rather than his own. He wants to see a robot survive the foundry's dirt and heat before he believes in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. With ten years the union can fight, but with two there's no time to win anything, and I'd be twenty-nine with a paid-off flat and nothing to get up for. What would help is a law that makes companies keep paying people they replace with robots, at least for a few years, and real money for retraining that you do on paid time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I blame. It's not the robots, and it's not the engineers. It's the people who'll own them and keep every bit of the savings, and the politicians who let them.

headlineQuote: I'd be twenty-nine with a paid-off flat and nothing to get up for.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old foundry moulder who has cast brake discs on the same line for nine years, owns his late grandmother's flat and has about nine months saved. He loves routine, his crew and his union, and has never used an AI tool. Across the scenarios he leans on collective action and politics rather than retraining, growing from calm in the plateau to alarmed when AGI is two years away. He blames the owners of the technology, not the technology itself, and is candid that he'd probably dig in rather than change.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture worries him most, because there would be no time for the union to win anything and he'd be left with nothing to get up for.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies keep paying people they replace with robots for a few years, and real retraining money for courses done on paid time.
